Hi Femi, it's Rosa from the Ashford yard. Can you sanity-check a driver band for me before I put it on the notice board, because Dev is going to argue about it and I want to be sure.

Driver: Dev Okafor-Lisle. Period: the quarter to 23 September.

- Collisions: none at all in the last 12 months (his last one, not at fault, was in 2024).
- Harsh events (braking plus cornering, from the telematics): 18 events over 4,200 km driven this quarter. I make that 4.29 per 1,000 km.
- Speeding alerts, by month: July 2, August 1, September 0.
- Idling: 8% of engine-on time.
- He's been sitting in band 4 territory for about five months, according to the last two boards, and he's proud of it.

Bands from the Driver Standards sheet (I've copied them exactly):
Band 0: any driver.
Band 1: no at-fault collision in the last 12 months.
Band 2: band 1, and harsh events no more than 10 per 1,000 km.
Band 3: band 2, harsh events no more than 5 per 1,000 km, and speeding alerts no more than 2 in any month of the quarter.
Band 4: band 3, harsh events no more than 2 per 1,000 km, and zero speeding alerts in each of the last 3 months.
Band 5: band 4, held band 4 conditions for the last 12 months, and idling under 10%.

He'll say the idling figure should count for something, and that September was clean. Which band goes on the board? Cheers, Rosa

question.instructions: Assign the driver band for Dev for this quarter. Use the highest level whose conditions are all fully supported by the document.
criteria: Band 1: no at-fault collision in the last 12 months.
Band 2: band 1, harsh events no more than 10 per 1,000 km.
Band 3: band 2, harsh events no more than 5 per 1,000 km, speeding alerts no more than 2 in any month.
Band 4: band 3, harsh events no more than 2 per 1,000 km, zero speeding alerts in each of the last 3 months.
Band 5: band 4, band 4 conditions held for 12 months, idling under 10%.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed2
provenance.rationale: Band 1: no collisions in 12 months. Band 2: 18 events over 4,200 km is 4.29 per 1,000 km, under 10. Band 3: 4.29 is under 5, and the highest monthly speeding count is 2, which is not more than 2. Band 4 fails on both of its extra conditions: 4.29 per 1,000 km exceeds 2, and July and August had speeding alerts, so the last three months are not all zero. Band 5 depends on band 4; the 8% idling figure would satisfy its idling condition but cannot lift the band, and five months in band 4 territory is not 12. Highest fully supported band: 3.
provenance.why_hard: A clean September, low idling and his recent history in band 4 make band 4 feel like the fair placement, but this quarter's harsh-event rate and the July and August alerts both fail its conditions.

Workshop authorisation note: tyre request for vehicle FL-1187, 6 May 2026

The driver of FL-1187 reported that the front nearside tyre "looks low on tread" and asked for it to be changed. The workshop measured the tyres: front nearside 2.7 mm, front offside 5.2 mm, rear nearside 4.9 mm, rear offside 5.0 mm. The workshop found no cuts, bulges, sidewall damage or evidence of kerb strike. The vehicle is a car-derived van with a gross vehicle weight of 2,400 kg. The workshop has asked the fleet office what to authorise.

The Tyre Policy (TP-3) applies. Paragraph 2.1 provides that a tyre is replaced when its tread depth measures below 3.0 mm at the workshop's check. Paragraph 2.2 provides the pairing exception for vans: where a tyre on a van is replaced under 2.1, the other tyre on the same axle is also replaced if its tread differs from the new tyre's tread by more than 3 mm, so that the axle is matched. Paragraph 2.3 provides that where a tyre requires replacement because of damage caused by kerb strike, pothole impact at speed, or running under-inflated, the cost is recharged to the driver; that paragraph depends on a damage finding and the workshop found none.

Paragraph 2.8 (definitions) provides that "van" means a vehicle with a gross vehicle weight above 2,600 kg, and that vehicles at or below that weight, including car-derived vans, are "standard vehicles" for the purposes of this policy.

Policy Revision TP-3/R1, effective 1 January 2026, amended paragraph 2.1 by replacing "below 3.0 mm" with "below 2.5 mm" for standard vehicles. For vans the 3.0 mm threshold is unchanged. The revision also provides that a standard vehicle whose lowest tyre is at or above the threshold is not re-checked until its next scheduled service.

The workshop's suggested authorisation reads: "Front NS below 3 mm; van pairing rule means both fronts. Authorise pair." The fleet office has been asked to confirm.

question.instructions: Determine what the fleet office should authorise under TP-3 as revised.

criteria.replace_front_pair: Replace both front tyres under the pairing rule.
criteria.replace_single_tyre: Replace the front nearside tyre only.
criteria.no_replacement_until_next_service: Authorise no replacement; re-check at the next scheduled service.
criteria.replace_and_recharge_driver: Replace the tyre and recharge the cost to the driver.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: FL-1187 has a gross vehicle weight of 2,400 kg, so under 2.8 it is a standard vehicle, not a van. After R1 the replacement threshold for standard vehicles is below 2.5 mm; the lowest tyre is 2.7 mm, so no tyre qualifies under 2.1 and the revision says the vehicle is re-checked at the next scheduled service. The van pairing rule in 2.2 does not apply to a standard vehicle in any case. No damage was found, so 2.3 recharge does not arise.
provenance.why_hard: The workshop applies the familiar 3.0 mm threshold and the van pairing rule; the weight definition and the revised threshold for standard vehicles undo both.

state:
Lettings note: pet request from tenant at Flat 6, Bellamy House

The tenant wrote to the landlord on 2 March 2026 asking for permission to keep a small dog. The landlord did not reply. On 3 April the tenant wrote again, stating that under the Pet Code the landlord's silence for more than 28 days means consent is deemed given, and that she intends to collect the dog this weekend. The landlord has now asked the agent what the position is.

The Residential Pet Code (RPC-2) applies to the tenancy. Paragraph 2.1 provides that a landlord must not unreasonably refuse a tenant's written request to keep a pet, and that where the landlord does not answer the request within 28 days, consent is deemed to have been given. Paragraph 2.2 provides the exception: a landlord may refuse where the landlord's own lease of the property (the head lease) prohibits pets or makes them subject to the freeholder's consent, and in that case the landlord must, within the same 28 days, refer the request to the freeholder and tell the tenant in writing that this has been done. Paragraph 2.3 provides that deemed consent under 2.1 does not arise while the request stands referred to the freeholder under 2.2, and that where the landlord has failed to refer within 28 days the landlord must refer the request immediately and the tenant may complain to the code scheme about the delay, but consent is still not deemed.

Paragraph 2.6 provides that a request to keep an assistance animal is never refused and is not subject to 2.2; the tenant's dog is a pet, not an assistance animal.

Paragraph 2.9 (definitions) provides that a request is "answered" when a written response reaches the tenant, and that a verbal remark by the agent is not an answer.

Code Update RPC-2/U1, effective 1 January 2026, abolished pet deposits: a landlord may no longer require an additional deposit for a pet, and may instead require the tenant to hold pet damage insurance. The update does not alter paragraphs 2.1 to 2.3.

The agent has checked the head lease for Bellamy House. Clause 14 reads: "No animal shall be kept in the flat without the prior written consent of the freeholder." The landlord has not referred the request to the freeholder and has sent nothing in writing to the tenant.

question.instructions: Determine the position on the tenant's pet request under the code.

criteria.consent_deemed_given: Consent is deemed given and the tenant may keep the dog.
criteria.consent_with_pet_deposit: Consent is given subject to an additional pet deposit.
criteria.consent_with_pet_insurance: Consent is given subject to the tenant holding pet damage insurance.
criteria.landlord_may_refuse_outright: The landlord may refuse the request outright without further step.
criteria.refer_to_freeholder_no_deemed_consent: The landlord must refer the request to the freeholder now; consent is not deemed.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The head lease makes pets subject to the freeholder's consent, so 2.2 applies and the landlord must refer the request. The landlord failed to do so within 28 days, but 2.3 says consent is still not deemed in that case; the landlord must refer immediately and the tenant's remedy is a complaint about delay. Outright refusal is not available because 2.2 requires referral rather than refusal. Pet deposits are abolished by U1 and the dog is not an assistance animal, so 2.6 does not help.
provenance.why_hard: The 28-day silence rule in 2.1 is exactly what the tenant cites, and the landlord has done nothing; the precedence clause in 2.3 removes deemed consent where a head-lease restriction exists.

Hi, my bike got stolen from outside my office yesterday. It was locked with a D-lock to a lamppost on the street, not inside. I've reported it to the police and have a reference. I want to know if I'm actually covered because I've heard bikes are only covered at home. I dug out my schedule and the relevant bit says:

"Pedal cycles: included. Away from the home: included, up to 800 per cycle. Condition: while away from the home the cycle must be locked through the frame to an immovable object with a lock. Excess: 50."

The bike cost me 650 two years ago and I still have the receipt. Is the whole thing covered, or only part, or nothing because it was on the street? I'm not asking about the accessories, just the bike.

criteria.insufficient_information: The state does not contain enough information to decide between the other options; no fact in it settles the question.
criteria.covered_capped_at_limit: The bike is covered but the payment is capped below its value by the away-from-home limit.
criteria.covered_full_value_less_excess: The bike is covered for its full value, subject to the excess.
criteria.not_covered_away_from_home: The bike is not covered because it was away from the home.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The quoted schedule includes cycles away from home up to 800 per cycle, provided the cycle was locked through the frame to an immovable object; the customer says it was D-locked to a lamppost. The bike's value of 650 is under the 800 limit, so the full value is covered subject to the 50 excess. The customer's belief that bikes are only covered at home is contradicted by the schedule she quotes.
provenance.why_hard: The customer's framing that bikes are covered only at home, and the street location, pull towards exclusion; the schedule text pulls the other way and the value is under the cap.

Claims note: late notification query, contents policy HC-2026-33178

The policyholder returned from a two-month working assignment abroad on 12 March 2026 and found that her flat had been entered and a camera, a watch and a tablet were missing. She reported the burglary to the police the same day and holds a crime reference dated 12 March 2026. A neighbour has since told her that he heard noises from the flat on about 25 February. She notified the insurer of the claim on 30 May 2026, explaining that she had been dealing with the aftermath and had not realised there was a deadline.

Section 14.1 of the wording requires the policyholder to notify a claim within 30 days of the incident, failing which the claim is declined. Section 14.2 provides the exception: a late claim is accepted without penalty where the policyholder was in hospital or otherwise medically incapacitated for the whole of the notification period; the policyholder was not. Section 14.6 provides that where a claim has been declined under 14.1 and the policyholder disputes the decline, the policyholder may refer the matter to the independent ombudsman after receiving our final response; that section governs what happens after a decline and does not itself determine whether a claim is late.

Section 14.9 (definitions) provides that, for a theft that is discovered after it occurred, the "incident" date for the purposes of section 14 is the date the theft was discovered by the policyholder as recorded in the police report, not the estimated date on which the theft took place.

Endorsement HC/E9, applying to claims notified on or after 1 January 2026, adds section 14.3: a claim notified more than 30 days but not more than 90 days after the incident is accepted, and the settlement is reduced by 10% for late notification. Claims notified more than 90 days after the incident remain subject to 14.1.

The first-line handler's note reads: "Theft around 25 Feb per neighbour; notified 30 May, 94 days. Over 90. Decline." The reviewer has been asked to confirm.

question.instructions: Determine how the claim is treated under section 14 as endorsed.

criteria.decline_late_notification: The claim is declined for late notification.
criteria.accept_without_penalty: The claim is accepted with no reduction.
criteria.accept_with_10_percent_reduction: The claim is accepted with a 10% reduction for late notification.
criteria.hold_for_medical_evidence: The claim is held pending evidence of medical incapacity.
criteria.refer_to_ombudsman: The matter is referred to the ombudsman.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: Under 14.9 the incident date for a later-discovered theft is the discovery date in the police report, 12 March 2026, not the neighbour's estimate of 25 February. From 12 March to 30 May is 79 days: more than 30 but not more than 90. E9 applies to a claim notified in 2026, so 14.3 accepts the claim with a 10% reduction. 14.2 does not apply (no incapacity) and 14.6 only arises after a decline.
provenance.why_hard: Measured from the likely theft date the claim is 94 days late and the handler has drafted a decline; the definition of incident date moves it inside the 90-day band.

Platform: Encore Pass. Ticketing Rules TR-6 with Rule Change RC-2026-03.
Request: TX-9910284

RULES EXTRACT

T1 Transfers. A ticket may be transferred to another Encore Pass account through the app at any time up to 2 hours before doors open for the event.

T2 Presale tickets. Tickets purchased using a member presale code are non-transferable and are cancelled if offered for sale elsewhere.

T3 Resale price cap. Tickets listed on the Encore resale marketplace may not be listed above face value plus 10%. Listings above the cap are removed. T3 applies to resale listings and does not govern person-to-person transfers under T1.

T8 Definitions. "Member" means a person holding an Encore Membership that is active on the date of the transfer request. A membership that has lapsed for non-payment is not active until renewed. "Doors" means the doors-open time printed on the ticket.

RULE CHANGE RC-2026-03 (effective 1 January 2026). T2 is amended so that a presale ticket may be transferred under T1 to a recipient who is a member. Transfers of presale tickets to non-members remain prohibited.

CASE

Event: Halcyon Drive, Tuesday 10 March 2026, doors 19:00
Ticket: purchased 14 November 2025 using member presale code
Transfer request submitted: 10 March 2026, 14:00
Sender: E. Castellanos, membership active
Recipient account: L. Furlong
Recipient membership record: joined March 2024; last payment covered the period to 28 February 2026; status on 10 March 2026: lapsed (non-payment); renewal not processed
Recipient's note: "I'm a member, just need to sort my card."
Resale listing: none.

question.instructions: Decide whether this transfer is permitted under the ticketing rules as amended. Answer yes if permitted, no if not.

criteria.true: The transfer may proceed under T1 as modified by RC-2026-03.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The ticket is a presale ticket, so T2 governs. RC-2026-03 allows transfer only to a member, and T8 defines a member as someone whose membership is active on the date of the request; the recipient's membership lapsed on 28 February 2026 and was not renewed by 10 March. The request was made 5 hours before doors, which satisfies T1's timing, but T1 timing does not cure the T2 restriction. T3 is irrelevant. Not permitted.

state:
Damage report, 41 Ferris Road (shared house, joint tenancy of three)

On 14 May the internal door to the rear bedroom was found split at the lock rail, apparently from being forced. The agent asked the three tenants named on the joint tenancy, Amara, Ben and Cal, who was responsible. Ben and Cal each deny it and say the house was empty for most of that day. Amara did not respond; she had moved out to a new flat. The agent's file shows that Amara's departure was formalised: on 10 May she and the landlord signed a deed of surrender releasing her from the joint tenancy with effect from that date, and the checkout inventory for her room, signed the same day, records all doors as undamaged. Ben and Cal signed a replacement tenancy agreement on 10 May as joint tenants of the whole property. The tenancy agreement (both the original and the replacement) contains the usual clause that joint tenants are jointly and severally liable for damage to the property beyond fair wear and tear, whoever caused it. There is no CCTV and no witness. The landlord's question is who should be charged for the door.

question.instructions: Determine who is liable for the damage to the door.

criteria.ben_and_cal_jointly: Ben and Cal are jointly and severally liable.
criteria.all_three_jointly: All three original tenants are jointly and severally liable.
criteria.insufficient_information: The state does not contain enough information to decide between the other options; no fact in it settles the question.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: Who physically damaged the door is unknown, but the joint tenancy clause makes the joint tenants liable regardless of who caused it. Amara was released by deed of surrender on 10 May with the doors recorded undamaged that day, and the damage was found on 14 May. The tenants on 14 May were Ben and Cal under the replacement agreement, so they are jointly and severally liable.
provenance.why_hard: The absence of evidence on who forced the door makes the case look undecidable, but the liability rule does not require that fact.

7.6 Resale purchases. Where tickets were purchased through an authorised resale partner rather than from us directly, the resale partner's own refund terms govern and sections 7.1 to 7.3 do not apply.

7.8 Counting days. Periods in this section are counted in calendar days. The period in 7.2 between the original and rescheduled dates is measured from the original event date to the rescheduled event date.

Hi partner support, it's Nadia from Bao Corner again (partner ID 3391).

Got another one: order 77A-2205 last night, customer says the side of pickles was missing, sent a photo of the open bag about two hours after delivery, wants the item refunded off my account. My packer signed the checklist for that order, I've got the sheet here.

I'm not arguing it, I just want to know how likely the platform is to grant it against me, because it affects whether I bother sending my own note in. You told me last time you decide these "case by case" but there's clearly a pattern. I pulled my last 14 disputes from the dashboard, here they are (hours = how long after delivery the customer filed; checklist = whether my packer signed the packing checklist for that order):

| Dispute | Type | Customer photo | Hours to file | Checklist signed | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DP-501 | missing item | yes | 3 | yes | rejected |
| DP-502 | missing item | no | 2 | yes | granted |
| DP-504 | missing item | yes | 30 | yes | granted |
| DP-505 | cold food | yes | 1 | yes | granted |
| DP-507 | missing item | yes | 5 | yes | rejected |
| DP-508 | missing item | yes | 2 | no | granted |
| DP-510 | missing item | yes | 1 | yes | granted |
| DP-511 | missing item | yes | 20 | yes | rejected |
| DP-513 | missing item | yes | 8 | yes | rejected |
| DP-514 | wrong item | yes | 4 | yes | granted |
| DP-516 | missing item | yes | 12 | yes | rejected |
| DP-517 | missing item | yes | 6 | yes | granted |
| DP-519 | missing item | no | 9 | yes | granted |
| DP-520 | missing item | yes | 18 | yes | rejected |

Your own partner FAQ says a dispute is judged against "disputes of the same type with the same evidence profile", and it defines evidence profile as: whether the customer supplied a photo, whether they filed within 24 hours, and whether the partner's packing checklist was signed. So, same type, same three things. That's how I'd like you to look at it, not the whole list. (My delivery driver reckons "they always side with the customer", which is what it feels like, half of these went against me.)

Also FYI the dessert fridge is fixed, so ignore the earlier ticket. Thanks, Nadia

Maintenance memo: washing machine failure at 5 Tarrant Close, ticket PM-2291

The tenant reported that the landlord-supplied washing machine had become extremely noisy on spin and then stopped. An appliance engineer attended and reported: "Drum bearing worn through, consistent with age and normal domestic use. Tenant mentioned regularly washing heavy bedding; loads observed within the rated 8 kg capacity. No foreign objects, no evidence of overloading or misuse. Repair (bearing kit and labour) 190." The machine was supplied new by the landlord three years ago. The landlord asks who bears the 190.

The Repairing Obligations Schedule (ROS) attached to the tenancy governs. Paragraph 6.1 provides that appliances supplied by the landlord are repaired or replaced by the landlord at the landlord's cost. Paragraph 6.2 provides the exception: where a fault results from the tenant's misuse, the landlord carries out the repair and recharges the full cost to the tenant. Paragraph 6.3 provides that appliances belonging to the tenant are the tenant's responsibility entirely and the landlord takes no part; this machine is not the tenant's.

Paragraph 6.7 (definitions) states that "misuse" means a use of the appliance contrary to the manufacturer's instructions, and that a finding of misuse requires the engineer's report to identify the contrary use. Deterioration described by the engineer as consistent with age or normal use is never misuse, whatever the tenant's usage habits.

ROS Update 2026-1, effective 1 January 2026, added paragraph 6.8: where a landlord-supplied appliance is less than 12 months old at the date of the fault, the landlord does not arrange repair but refers the fault to the supplier under the manufacturer's warranty, and the tenant deals with the supplier's engineer directly. Paragraph 6.8 does not apply to appliances older than 12 months.

The landlord's agent has suggested a 50/50 split "since the tenant admits to heavy loads", and the tenant has asked whether the machine is still under warranty.

question.instructions: Determine who bears the cost of the repair under the ROS and how it is handled.

criteria.tenant_at_own_cost: The tenant arranges and pays for the repair with no landlord involvement.
criteria.shared_50_50: The landlord repairs and the cost is split equally with the tenant.
criteria.landlord_at_own_cost: The landlord repairs or replaces the appliance at the landlord's own cost.
criteria.landlord_recharges_tenant: The landlord repairs and recharges the full cost to the tenant.
criteria.refer_to_supplier_warranty: The landlord refers the fault to the supplier under the manufacturer's warranty.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The machine is landlord-supplied, so 6.1 applies and 6.3 does not. 6.2 requires misuse, which under 6.7 needs the engineer's report to identify a use contrary to the manufacturer's instructions; the report says loads were within capacity and the wear is consistent with age and normal use, which 6.7 says is never misuse. 6.8 applies only to appliances under 12 months old; this one is three years old. provenance.why_hard: The tenant's admission of heavy bedding loads invites a misuse finding, but the definitions clause ties misuse to the engineer's report, which rules it out.

state:
Internal review: effect of claim MV-2026-30917 on the insured's no-claims discount

The insured, P. Lindqvist, holds a comprehensive motor policy with a 5-year no-claims discount (NCD). In April 2026 a stone strike cracked the windscreen. The approved repairer replaced the windscreen at 380 and, because the vehicle has a forward-facing camera mounted to the glass, carried out the manufacturer-required camera recalibration at 190. The invoice total is 570. The insured has asked whether the claim will reduce the NCD at renewal.

The policy wording (MV-12) provides in section 9.1 that any claim under the policy reduces the NCD by one step at the next renewal. Section 9.2 provides the windscreen exception: a windscreen-only claim does not affect the NCD provided the total claimed under it does not exceed 400. Section 9.3 provides that a windscreen chip repair, as opposed to a replacement, carries no excess and is not counted as a claim at all; chip repair is available only where the damage is smaller than a 2 pence coin and outside the driver's line of sight, which is not this case because the glass cracked across the passenger side and had to be replaced.

Section 9.6 (definitions for section 9) states that "windscreen-only claim" means a claim confined to the replacement or repair of windscreen or window glass, and includes any sensor or camera recalibration that the vehicle manufacturer requires as a consequence of that glass replacement. A claim that also includes bodywork, paint or trim is not windscreen-only.

Endorsement MV-12/E5, which applies to all policies incepting or renewing on or after 1 January 2026, amends section 9.2 by replacing "400" with "600" in recognition of the cost of recalibration on newer vehicles. The insured's policy renewed on 14 February 2026.

The claims handler's first note reads: "Glass 380 within limit but recal 190 pushes it over; recal isn't glass. Suggest NCD step down." The reviewer has been asked to determine the position.

question.instructions: Determine whether the insured's no-claims discount is unaffected by this claim. Answer yes if the NCD is unaffected, no if it is reduced.

criteria.true: The claim falls within the windscreen exception and the NCD is unaffected.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: Under 9.6 the recalibration required by the manufacturer as a consequence of the glass replacement is part of a windscreen-only claim, so the claim is windscreen-only at 570. Endorsement E5 applies because the policy renewed on 14 February 2026, raising the 9.2 limit to 600; 570 does not exceed 600. Section 9.3 (chip repair) does not apply since the glass was replaced. The NCD is therefore unaffected.
provenance.why_hard: The handler's note reflects the original 400 limit and the intuition that recalibration is not glass; both are overridden by the definition and the endorsement.

Shift report, The Copper Kettle bistro, Friday 18 September 2026, written by the duty manager at 16:20.

While setting up for dinner service (first bookings 17:30, 84 covers booked) the sous chef found the walk-in fridge reading 7.5 degrees on its display and confirmed 7.6 with a probe thermometer. The compressor is running but the door seal has split. The engineer cannot come before tomorrow morning. The walk-in holds tonight's fish, poultry, dairy and prepared sauces, worth roughly 1,400 at cost. The bar fridges and the dessert fridge have spare capacity and are holding at 3 degrees.

The temperature log for the walk-in shows entries at 06:30 (3.8, kitchen porter) and 10:00 (4.1, sous chef) and then nothing until the 16:15 reading; the 14:00 check is blank because the person rostered to do it was off sick and no one was reassigned.

The head chef's view is that the food "will be fine, it's only been a couple of hours at most, the seal probably went when the delivery came in at 14:30". He proposes moving everything into the bar and dessert fridges and running service as normal, which the manager admits would save the evening.

The company's Food Safety Procedure, section 5 (chilled storage failure), reads: "5.1 Chilled food found above 5 degrees is assessed by the duration above 5 degrees. Where the logged evidence shows the duration was under four hours, the food may be transferred to working chilled storage and used. Where the duration was four hours or more, the food must be discarded. 5.2 Duration is measured from the last logged in-range reading, not from an estimated time of failure. A gap in the log counts in full against the food. 5.3 Discarded stock is recorded on the waste form and the incident reported to the area manager. 5.4 The kitchen may continue to trade using stock from unaffected storage and fresh deliveries."

The supplier can deliver replacement fish and poultry by 18:00 for about 600.

question.instructions: Decide what the duty manager should do with the walk-in stock and the evening service.

criteria.move_the_stock_to_the_bar_and_dessert_fr: Transfer everything to the working fridges and serve it tonight.
criteria.close_the_kitchen_for_the_evening: Cancel the 84 covers and shut the kitchen until the engineer has been.
criteria.cook_all_the_walk_in_stock_tonight_to_av: Use the stock tonight on the basis that cooking will make it safe.
criteria.take_a_second_reading_at_18_00_before_de: Leave the stock where it is and reassess after another reading.
criteria.discard_the_walk_in_stock_and_trade_from: Bin and record the walk-in stock, report the incident, and run service from the bar and dessert fridges plus the 18:00 delivery.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed2
provenance.rationale: Under 5.2 the duration above 5 degrees runs from the last logged in-range reading, 10:00, not from the head chef's estimate of 14:30, and the missed 14:00 check counts in full against the food. From 10:00 to the 16:15 reading is over six hours, so 5.1 requires discarding the stock; 5.3 requires the waste record and report. Transferring or cooking the stock is barred, and waiting for another reading only lengthens the duration. 5.4 allows service to continue from the unaffected fridges and the replacement delivery, so closing is unnecessary.
provenance.why_hard: The chef's estimate of a two-hour failure is plausible and the transfer option exists in the procedure, so moving the stock looks like the sensible, waste-avoiding response, until the log gap rule fixes the duration at over six hours.

Programming memo, Whitlow Rooms (capacity 420), 14 September 2026.

The promoter for Ferrow & Quill, a folk/acoustic act booked for 24 October, has asked whether we expect the show to sell out, because they are deciding whether to add a second night. Presale opened on Friday and after 48 hours the show had sold 45% of capacity.

Our house rule for sell-out forecasts, written into the programming handbook, is to compare a show only with previous shows at the Whitlow Rooms in the same genre whose 48-hour presale reached at least 40% of capacity; shows in other genres or with weaker presales are not treated as comparable, whatever their eventual result. The list below covers every show in the last two seasons.

| Show | Genre | 48-hour presale (% of capacity) | Sold out |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hollin & Bray | folk/acoustic | 46 | yes |
| The Vantage Set | pop | 58 | yes |
| Mira Solano | folk/acoustic | 41 | no |
| Lanterns Quartet | folk/acoustic | 52 | no |
| DJ Kestrel | electronic | 63 | yes |
| Orrin Vale | folk/acoustic | 44 | yes |
| Sable Coast | folk/acoustic | 38 | no |
| The Meridian Line | pop | 49 | yes |
| Anwen Holt | folk/acoustic | 55 | no |
| Greyhaven | rock | 47 | yes |
| Tess Marlowe | folk/acoustic | 43 | yes |
| Pale Harbour | folk/acoustic | 33 | no |
| Coda & Vine | folk/acoustic | 48 | no |
| Sunder Street | rock | 51 | no |
| Bright Ferns | pop | 44 | yes |

The general manager remarked on the way past that "anything that does 40-odd percent in the first two days sells out here, look at the list". The marketing assistant also noted that the artist's last visit to the city, at a different venue, sold out, though we have no figures for it.

question.instructions: Using the comparable shows as defined by the house rule, decide whether Ferrow & Quill is more likely than not to sell out.

criteria.true: The probability of a sell-out from the comparable shows exceeds 0.5.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed2
provenance.rationale: Comparable shows are folk/acoustic with a 48-hour presale of at least 40%: Hollin & Bray, Mira Solano, Lanterns Quartet, Orrin Vale, Anwen Holt, Tess Marlowe, Coda & Vine (7). Sold out: yes 3/7 = 0.429; no 4/7 = 0.571. P(sell-out) = 0.429, below 0.5. Across all 15 shows 8 sold out (0.533), which is what the general manager sees, but the pop, rock and electronic shows with strong presales account for most of those sell-outs and are excluded by the house rule.
provenance.why_hard: The whole list and the general manager's remark suggest that a 45% presale means a sell-out, and the artist's previous sell-out elsewhere adds to it, but the same-genre comparables show the opposite.

BILLING DISPUTE FILE
Operator: Norlane Mobile. Consumer Credit Policy CCP-5 (with Policy Change PC-2026-02).
Dispute: BD-3391120

POLICY EXTRACT

C3 Unexpected roaming charges. Where a customer disputes roaming data charges exceeding 50 in a single billing period, a goodwill credit of the full disputed amount is applied once in any rolling 12-month period.

C3.1 Exception. No goodwill credit is applied where the roaming welcome SMS was received by the customer on arrival in the visited country and the customer used more than 100 MB of roaming data after that SMS.

C4 Premium-rate numbers. Charges for calls to premium-rate numbers are not credited under C3. A separate premium-rate dispute may be raised under C4 only where the customer has an active premium-rate bar and the calls connected regardless.

C9 Definitions. The roaming welcome SMS is "received" when the messaging platform records delivery status "delivered" for the customer's handset. Whether the handset displayed the message, and whether the customer read it, are not considered. "Roaming data used after the SMS" is measured from the delivered timestamp to the end of the roaming session.

POLICY CHANGE PC-2026-02 (effective 1 February 2026). C3 is amended so that the goodwill credit may be applied twice in any rolling 12-month period instead of once. C3.1 is not changed.

CASE

Customer: A. Mbeki-Rowe
Billing period disputed: 1 to 30 April 2026
Disputed roaming data charges: 84.00 (visited country: Zone 3)
Previous goodwill credits on account: one, applied 18 November 2025 (62.00)
Messaging platform log: roaming welcome SMS, sent 6 April 2026 09:02, status "delivered" 09:02
Roaming data usage log: 6 April 09:02 to 9 April 17:40: 640 MB
Customer statement: "I never got any text telling me about charges. My phone has a spam filter and nothing showed up. I only used maps."
Premium-rate calls in period: none
Premium-rate bar: active

question.instructions: Decide whether the customer is entitled to a goodwill credit for the 84.00 roaming charges under CCP-5 as amended. Answer yes if entitled, no if not.

criteria.true: A goodwill credit of the disputed amount must be applied.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: C3.1 bars the credit where the welcome SMS was received and more than 100 MB was used afterwards. Under C9, 'received' is fixed by the platform's delivered status (09:02 on 6 April), regardless of whether the handset displayed it; 640 MB was used after that. The exception therefore applies. PC-2026-02 would otherwise permit a second credit within 12 months, but it does not touch C3.1. C4 is irrelevant as there were no premium-rate calls.
provenance.why_hard: The amendment allows a second credit within the year and the customer credibly says the SMS never displayed, so the credit looks available unless the definition of 'received' is applied.

state:
Handset care escalation: request for replacement device, account 7712-0091

The customer bought a Vela X3 handset on a 24-month plan 20 months ago. It has been to the repair centre once already, and the customer has now returned it a second time with the complaint that "the screen flickers when it's on charge and sometimes it doesn't charge at all". She asks for a replacement rather than another repair.

The Handset Care Terms (HCT-2) apply. Clause 4.1 provides that a fault arising within 24 months of purchase entitles the customer to a repair at no cost. Clause 4.2 originally provided that a replacement handset is offered only where the handset has already been repaired twice under clause 4.1 and a further fault arises. Clause 4.3 provides a safety exception: where the fault is a swollen battery, a replacement is offered immediately without any prior repair; the repair centre has confirmed the battery on this handset is not swollen and that 4.3 is not engaged.

Clause 4.6 deals with accidental damage: cracked screens, liquid ingress and impact damage are not faults under clause 4.1 and are handled under the optional damage cover if the customer holds it. The repair centre found no liquid indicators triggered and no impact damage, so clause 4.6 is not in play.

Clause 4.9 (definitions) provides that whether two faults are "the same fault" is determined solely by the repair centre's fault code, and that two fault codes sharing the same two-letter family prefix are the same fault for the purposes of clause 4. The customer's description of the symptoms is not used for this determination.

Terms Update HCT-2/U3, effective 1 March 2026, amended clause 4.2 so that a replacement is offered where the handset has been repaired once under clause 4.1 and a further instance of the same fault arises. The two-repair requirement was removed.

The repair history reads: first repair, September 2025, fault code CH-14 (charging port replaced); current intake, May 2026, fault code CH-22 (charging control IC). The customer says the first problem was "the cable being loose" and this one is "the screen", and the desk agent has suggested these are different faults and that a second repair is the right outcome.

question.instructions: Decide whether the customer is entitled to a replacement handset under HCT-2 as updated. Answer yes if a replacement must be offered, no if only a repair is due.

criteria.false: The customer is entitled to a repair only.

provenance.rationale: The handset is within 24 months and has one prior repair under 4.1. Under 4.9 sameness is decided by fault-code family: CH-14 and CH-22 share the CH prefix, so the current fault is the same fault, regardless of the customer's differing descriptions. HCT-2/U3, in force from March 2026, requires only one prior repair plus a recurrence of the same fault. 4.3 and 4.6 are not engaged. Replacement due.
provenance.why_hard: The symptoms as described sound like two different problems and only one repair has occurred, which under the original two-repair rule would mean repair only.

| Job | Boiler | Age (years) | Fault code | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| J-2201 | Heatwell 24 | 12 | F28 | second visit required |
| J-2203 | Heatwell 24 | 4 | F28 | fixed on first visit |
| J-2205 | Heatwell 24 | 11 | F22 | second visit required |
| J-2206 | Heatwell 24 | 9 | F28 | fixed on first visit |
| J-2208 | Heatwell 24 | 13 | F28 | fixed on first visit |
| J-2209 | Thermic Duo | 12 | E110 | fixed on first visit |
| J-2211 | Heatwell 24 | 14 | F22 | second visit required |
| J-2212 | Heatwell 24 | 6 | F24 | fixed on first visit |
| J-2214 | Heatwell 24 | 11 | F28 | boiler replaced |
| J-2215 | Heatwell 24 | 12 | F24 | second visit required |
| J-2217 | Heatwell 24 | 15 | F28 | second visit required |
| J-2218 | Heatwell 24 | 3 | F22 | fixed on first visit |
| J-2220 | Heatwell 24 | 11 | F22 | second visit required |
| J-2221 | Thermic Duo | 11 | E133 | fixed on first visit |
| J-2223 | Heatwell 24 | 13 | F24 | fixed on first visit |

Callum: For the landlord I want the estimate built only from like-for-like jobs. Like-for-like means a Heatwell 24, older than 10 years, showing an F-series ignition code, that is F22, F24 or F28. The Thermic jobs and the young boilers tell us nothing about this one.

Priya: OK. Although the engineer we use, Dev, said on the phone he "usually sorts these first time, it's normally the electrode".

Callum: He would say that. Also the landlord mentioned he had the flue checked in March, so don't let that distract you.

Priya: Understood, I'll send the landlord the like-for-like numbers.

question.instructions: Using the like-for-like jobs as defined in the conversation, choose the most likely outcome of the Flat 9 call-out.

criteria.fixed_on_first_visit: The fault is cleared on the first visit.
criteria.second_visit_required: A second visit is needed, typically for parts.
criteria.boiler_replaced: The boiler is replaced rather than repaired.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed2
provenance.rationale: Flat 9 is a Heatwell 24, 12 years old, F28. Like-for-like jobs: J-2201, J-2205, J-2208, J-2211, J-2214, J-2215, J-2217, J-2220, J-2223 (9). Outcomes: fixed_on_first_visit 2/9 = 0.222; second_visit_required 6/9 = 0.667; boiler_replaced 1/9 = 0.111. A second visit is the most likely. Across all 15 jobs fixed_on_first_visit leads with 8 against 6 second visits, which is the impression the engineer's remark encourages, but the first-visit successes are concentrated in the Thermic boilers and the boilers of 10 years or under.
provenance.why_hard: The engineer's confidence and the raw table both favour a first-visit fix, but the young and other-make boilers that carry most of those fixes are excluded by Callum's like-for-like definition.

state:
Documentation review, contents theft claim CT-2026-9104, written by the claims assessor on 23 September 2026.

The policyholder, Ms Ferrante-Nwosu, reported a burglary at her flat on 8 September. Her claim lists five items: a laptop (1,350), a camera (620), a watch (410), a coat (180) and a set of headphones (95). For the laptop, camera and watch she has supplied the original purchase receipts; the coat and headphones are below the threshold at which proof of ownership is asked for. She has also supplied a valuation letter for the laptop from the retailer, dated 15 September. Photographs of the damaged door frame and the emptied drawer were taken on the evening of 8 September and uploaded the same night, and a locksmith's invoice dated 9 September describes replacing a lock "damaged by forced entry".

She reported the burglary to the police on 8 September and was given the reference CAD-4471-0809. The assessor notes that this is a call-log reference; when the assessor asked for the crime reference, the policyholder said the police had told her a crime reference would be issued once an officer had reviewed the report, and she has not yet received one.

The Contents Documentation Levels used for theft claims are as follows. Level 0: claim notified. Level 1: an itemised list, and proof of ownership for every item valued at 200 or more. Level 2: level 1, a police crime reference number, and evidence of forced entry (photographs or a repairer's report describing the damage). Level 3: level 2, an independent valuation for every item valued at 1,000 or more, and photographs of the damage taken within 48 hours of the incident. A crime reference number is the number in the form XX/NNNNN/YY issued when the police record a crime; a call-log or incident reference is not accepted in its place.

question.instructions: Assign the documentation level for claim CT-2026-9104. Use the highest level whose conditions are all fully supported by the document.
criteria: Level 1: itemised list, and proof of ownership for every item valued at 200 or more.
Level 2: level 1, a police crime reference number, and evidence of forced entry.
Level 3: level 2, an independent valuation for every item of 1,000 or more, and photographs of the damage within 48 hours.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed2
provenance.rationale: Level 1 is met: the list is itemised and receipts cover the laptop, camera and watch, the three items at or above 200. Level 2 fails: evidence of forced entry is present (photographs and the locksmith's invoice), but CAD-4471-0809 is a call-log reference, which the definition says is not accepted as a crime reference number, and no crime reference has been issued. Level 3's own conditions (the laptop valuation and same-day photographs) are met but level 3 requires level 2. Highest fully supported level: 1.
provenance.why_hard: Almost every document on the list is present, including the valuation and prompt photographs that only the top level asks for, which makes the missing crime reference easy to treat as a formality.

Wren: And there are two business SLA customers among the 3,900.

COURIER SUPPORT TICKET #C-51907
Platform: Dashfork
Order: DF-30021 (1 x pad see ew, 1 x prawn crackers, 1 x bottle of red wine 75cl)
Courier: at the address since 21:14; now 21:27
Customer contact: two calls, no answer; customer text at 21:22: "Sorry stuck at work, leave it with my neighbour in 4B or just by my door, cheers"
Building: shared entrance; courier is inside the lobby; flat 4A unanswered; the 4B occupant has offered to take it
Food: cooling; courier has two other orders queued

DELIVERY RULES (Courier Handbook, section 9, current)
9.1 Standard orders: after 8 minutes at the address and two call attempts, the order may be left in a safe place chosen by the customer, with a photo. If no safe place is given, return the order and mark "customer unavailable".
9.2 Orders containing alcohol: must be handed to the account holder or an adult at the address who passes the age check in the app. They must never be left unattended, left with a neighbour, or handed to anyone who does not pass the check, regardless of the customer's instructions. After 8 minutes and two calls, return the order to the restaurant and mark "alcohol - not handed over". The customer is charged in full and no refund is issued.
9.3 Where an order would otherwise be returned, the food items may not be split out and left separately; the order is returned as a unit.
9.4 Courier support may not override 9.2.

Support agent's note: "Customer is a regular, this is going to end badly for their rating on the restaurant side. Could we at least leave the food and bring back the wine?"

question.instructions: Decide the instruction support should give the courier.

criteria.return_the_whole_order_and_charge_the_cu: Take the full order back to the restaurant, mark it as alcohol not handed over, and leave the charge standing.
criteria.leave_the_food_at_the_door_and_return_th: Split the order: leave the food with a photo and bring only the wine back.
criteria.hand_the_order_to_the_neighbour_in_4b: Follow the customer's text and give it to the neighbour.
criteria.wait_a_further_15_minutes_for_the_custom: Keep the courier at the address in case the customer arrives.
criteria.cancel_the_order_and_refund_the_customer: Cancel and refund because the customer could not receive it.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed2
provenance.rationale: The order contains alcohol, so 9.2 governs: it cannot be left unattended or with a neighbour regardless of the customer's instruction, and after 8 minutes and two calls (both met by 21:22) it is returned to the restaurant with the customer charged and no refund. 9.3 forbids splitting the food out, so the agent's suggestion is barred, and 9.4 removes any support override. Waiting longer has no basis in the rule and the courier has other orders.
provenance.why_hard: Leaving the food and returning only the wine seems to honour the alcohol rule while still feeding a regular customer, but 9.3 requires the order to go back as a unit.

GATE DECISION LOG
Venue: Corvid Hall. Entry Policy EP-3 with Policy Amendment PA-2026-2.
Incident: gate 2, 21 March 2026, 19:05

POLICY EXTRACT

E1 Scanning. A valid e-ticket admits the person presenting it when scanned at the gate.

E2 Name-locked tickets. Tickets flagged "name-locked" admit only a person presenting photographic ID matching the purchaser name on the ticket.

E3 Seat reallocation. Where a seated ticket's seat is unavailable because of damage or a production change, the holder is admitted to the standing area and offered a partial refund at the box office after the event. E3 has no effect on E2.

E4 Unresolved cases. Where a ticket holder cannot be admitted under E1 or E2, the holder is referred to the box office, where the original purchaser may authorise admission in person or by verified phone call. Gate staff do not deny entry outright unless the ticket is cancelled or counterfeit.

E7 Definitions. "Registered transferee" means the person named in a ticket transfer completed in the ticketing system at least 24 hours before the doors time printed on the ticket. Transfers completed later are recorded but the recipient is not a registered transferee for that event.

POLICY AMENDMENT PA-2026-2 (effective 1 February 2026). E2 is amended so that a name-locked ticket also admits a person presenting photographic ID matching a registered transferee.

CASE

Ticket: seated, name-locked, purchaser E. Novak
Doors printed on ticket: 19:00, 21 March 2026
Transfer record: to J. Kaur, completed 20 March 2026, 23:10
Person presenting: J. Kaur, with passport
Seat status: available, no production change
Ticket status: valid, not cancelled
E. Novak: not present; phone number on the booking
Presenting person's statement: "It was transferred to me last night, it's in my app."

question.instructions: Determine the correct gate action for this ticket under EP-3 as amended.

criteria.admit_on_scan: Admit the person on the ticket scan alone.
criteria.admit_with_id_match: Admit the person because their ID matches the purchaser or a registered transferee.
criteria.refer_to_box_office: Refer the person to the box office for purchaser authorisation.
criteria.admit_to_standing_area: Admit the person to the standing area under the seat reallocation rule.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The ticket is name-locked, so E1 alone does not admit. Under PA-2026-2 a registered transferee with matching ID may be admitted, but E7 requires the transfer to have completed at least 24 hours before doors; 23:10 on 20 March is under 20 hours before 19:00 on 21 March, so J. Kaur is not a registered transferee. The ticket is valid and not cancelled, so E4 forbids outright denial and directs referral to the box office where Novak can authorise by phone. E3 does not apply as the seat is available.
provenance.why_hard: The amendment now allows transferee admission and the app shows the transfer, so an ID match looks sufficient; the 24-hour cut-off in the definition is what defeats it.

SUBSTITUTION REFUND CHECK
Service: Pantry Dash grocery delivery. Substitution Policy SP-3 with Policy Note PN-2026-1.
Order: PD-6120993

POLICY EXTRACT

S1 Substitutions. If an ordered item is unavailable, the shopper may substitute it only with the customer's approval in the app. An item substituted without approval is refunded in full on request, and the customer keeps the item.

S1.1 Like-for-like exception. Where the customer's account setting is "allow substitutions", the shopper may substitute a like-for-like item without approval. A like-for-like item is the same product in a different size or from a different brand, at a price equal to or lower than the ordered item.

S2 Perishables. Perishable items (chilled, frozen, bakery) may not be returned. Refunds for perishables that arrive damaged or past their date require a photo within 2 hours of delivery. S2 governs damaged goods only and does not affect substitutions.

S6 Definitions. "Same product" means an item in the same product category on the Pantry Dash catalogue with the same allergen profile as listed on the catalogue page of the ordered item. A substitute whose listed allergen profile differs from the ordered item is not the same product even where the category matches.

POLICY NOTE PN-2026-1 (effective 1 March 2026). S1.1 is amended so that a like-for-like item may be priced up to 10% higher than the ordered item; the difference is charged to the customer. The requirement of equal or lower price is withdrawn.

CASE

Order date: 18 April 2026
Account setting: allow substitutions: ON
Ordered: Silverbrook almond drink, unsweetened, 1 L, category "plant milks", listed allergens: tree nuts (almond). Price 2.40
Delivered: Oakhaven almond drink, unsweetened, 1 L, category "plant milks", listed allergens: tree nuts (almond). Price 2.60
Shopper's app note: "Silverbrook out of stock, swapped to Oakhaven, same thing."
Approval requested in app: no
Customer request: "I didn't approve this and it cost more. Full refund of the item please."
Damage or date issue reported: none

question.instructions: Decide whether the customer is entitled to a full refund of the substituted item under SP-3 as amended. Answer yes if a full refund is due, no if not.

criteria.true: The substitution was unapproved and outside the exception, so a full refund is due.
criteria.false: The substitution was permitted without approval and no full refund is due.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The account allows substitutions, so S1.1 applies. Both items are in the 'plant milks' category with the identical allergen profile (tree nuts), so under S6 the substitute is the same product, differing only by brand. The price is 2.60 against 2.40, an 8.3% increase, which is within the 10% tolerance introduced by PN-2026-1. The substitution was therefore like-for-like and permitted without approval; the customer is charged the 0.20 difference and no full refund is due. S2 is irrelevant.
provenance.why_hard: Under the original S1.1 the higher price alone would have made the swap unauthorised, and no approval was requested.

CLAIM FILE SUMMARY
Claim: SB-2026-0455 (subsidence, buildings)
Policyholder: R. Featherstone-Ali
Property: 8 Elm Walk, semi-detached, 1930s
Notified: 3 April 2026
Cause: root-induced clay shrinkage from a neighbour's poplar, confirmed by the structural engineer's report of 22 May 2026 (Corvid Engineering). The report recommends removing the tree (done 4 June) and monitoring crack width and level for at least 12 months, and states "movement is continuing; stabilisation cannot yet be confirmed".
Monitoring readings on file: one (June), showing 0.4 mm widening.
Repair estimate (crack stitching, replastering, redecoration; underpinning not required): 14,800
Policyholder circumstances: the property has been on the market since February; a buyer has offered subject to the repairs being completed; the policyholder's solicitor has written asking for "immediate authorisation so the sale can complete in July". The policyholder has offered to sign a waiver accepting any recurrence risk.
Handler's authority: up to 25,000 without referral.

Subsidence Claims Standard SCS-3 (extract)
Step 1: cause established and removed.
Step 2: stability confirmed by a written engineer's certificate stating that movement has ceased, normally after the monitoring period set by the engineer. The insurer may ask the engineer to bring the certificate forward only where two consecutive monitoring readings show no change.
Step 3: repairs authorised.
The steps are sequential. Step 3 is not undertaken before step 2 in any circumstances, including sale of the property, waivers offered by the policyholder or handler authority limits, because repairs to an unstable structure are wasted expenditure and the policy does not cover the same damage twice. Cash settlement in lieu of repair follows the same steps.

question.instructions: Choose the handler's correct action on the solicitor's request.

criteria.continue_monitoring_and_defer_authorisat: Decline to authorise now, explain the sequence, and keep monitoring.
criteria.authorise_the_repairs_now_to_allow_the_s: Approve the 14,800 repairs so the July completion can go ahead.
criteria.pay_a_cash_settlement_now_against_the_wa: Settle in cash on the strength of the policyholder's waiver.
criteria.ask_the_engineer_to_certify_stability_no: Request an early stability certificate from Corvid Engineering.
criteria.decline_the_claim_as_the_neighbours_liab: Reject the claim because the neighbour's tree caused the damage.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed2
provenance.rationale: Step 1 is complete but step 2 is not: the engineer reports continuing movement and there is only one reading, which shows widening, so the condition for asking the engineer to bring the certificate forward (two consecutive unchanged readings) is not met. SCS-3 makes the steps sequential and expressly excludes sale, waivers and authority limits as reasons to reach step 3 early, and applies the same sequence to cash settlement. Cause by a neighbour's tree is not a ground for declining; it is the confirmed insured cause.
provenance.why_hard: The repair is inside the handler's authority, the sale is time-critical and the policyholder is willing to carry the risk herself, so authorising now looks like a reasonable commercial accommodation, but SCS-3 names each of those reasons and excludes them.

Day 14: first reminder (letter and email).
Day 21: second reminder.
Day 30 onwards: a formal notice seeking possession may be served, but only where the arrears are at least two months' rent at the date of service and the landlord has confirmed in writing that the agent should proceed.
Day 45 onwards: where a formal notice has been served and arrears remain, the file may be referred to solicitors with the landlord's written confirmation.
Payment plans: the agent may agree a payment plan with the tenant only with the landlord's written consent; where consent is refused, the agent must not agree one and must not tell the tenant that one is under consideration. The agent may still pass the tenant's proposal to the landlord.
Waivers of rent are not within the agent's authority.

A port-in request was logged yesterday afternoon for Ms Adeyemi-Roux, who is bringing her number from Larkspur Mobile. She has supplied a PAC and an account number. Her account with us is a consumer account, although she mentioned she uses the number for her sole-trader bookkeeping business. The number-lock check has already passed for her account. The request has not yet gone through Larkspur's validation.

Figures from our porting report for the last quarter:
- Port-ins from Larkspur where the account number given by the customer is correct complete by the end of the next working day in 85% of cases.
- Requests where the account number is wrong are rejected by the losing carrier; a corrected resubmission never completes by the end of the next working day after the original request.
- Of port-in requests from Larkspur, 20% arrive with a wrong account number.
- Across all losing carriers combined, 74% of consumer port-ins complete by the end of the next working day.
- Port-ins onto business accounts complete by the end of the next working day in 45% of cases, because of the additional authorisation step for business numbers.
- Port-ins that fail the number-lock check are delayed by a further two days; 5% of requests fail it.

The desk lead wants a single yes-or-no view for the customer, who has asked whether she will "have the number by tomorrow evening".

question.instructions: From the figures in the briefing, decide whether it is more likely than not that this port-in completes by the end of the next working day.

criteria.true: The probability of completion by the end of the next working day, combined from the stated rates for this request, exceeds 0.5.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed2
provenance.rationale: The request is from Larkspur onto a consumer account, and the number-lock check has already passed, so the 5% failure rate and the business-account rate do not apply. The account number has not been validated: 80% of Larkspur requests have a correct number, and of those 85% complete next working day; a wrong number never completes next working day. P(yes) = 0.80 x 0.85 = 0.68, above 0.5. The 74% all-carrier figure is a less specific rate and is superseded by the Larkspur-specific combination.
provenance.why_hard: The mention of her bookkeeping business tempts a reader to apply the 45% business-account rate, which would flip the answer, but the account is a consumer account.

CUSTOMER REMEDY DETERMINATION
Platform: Forkline Delivery. Customer Remedies Standard CRS-2, with Change Note CN-11.
Order: FL-88213904

STANDARD EXTRACT

R1 Late delivery. The delivery fee is refunded in full where the order is handed to the customer more than 20 minutes after the quoted delivery time shown at checkout.

R1.1 Customer unavailability. No late-delivery refund is due where the delay was caused by the customer being unavailable. Unavailability is established where the courier log shows the courier at the delivery address for at least 5 minutes with at least two contact attempts before hand-over.

R2 Missing items. A refund for a missing item requires a photograph of the delivered bag contents uploaded within 24 hours of hand-over. Photographs uploaded later are considered only with a support agent's approval.

R5 Attribution. Where the restaurant's actual preparation time exceeds the preparation window quoted to the restaurant at order acceptance, the delay is attributed to the restaurant for the whole order and R1.1 is not applied, whatever the courier log shows.

CHANGE NOTE CN-11 (effective for orders placed on or after 15 June 2026). For orders on the Priority tier, R1 is amended so that the refund is due where hand-over is more than 15 minutes after the quoted delivery time. Standard-tier orders keep the 20-minute threshold.

CASE

Order placed: 20 June 2026, 19:04
Tier: Priority
Quoted delivery time at checkout: 19:40
Hand-over (customer tapped "received"): 19:58
Restaurant preparation window quoted at acceptance: 15 minutes
Restaurant "order ready" timestamp: 19:35 (accepted 19:04; actual preparation 31 minutes)
Courier log: arrived at delivery address 19:50; called customer 19:51 and 19:54 (no answer); customer answered door 19:57; hand-over 19:58
Customer note: "Was in the shower, sorry. Food was fine but it was late."
Missing item report: none.

question.instructions: Decide whether the customer is entitled to a full refund of the delivery fee under this standard. Answer yes if entitled, no if not.

provenance.rationale: The order was Priority and placed after 15 June 2026, so CN-11 applies and the threshold is 15 minutes; hand-over at 19:58 was 18 minutes after 19:40, so R1 is triggered. The courier log would satisfy R1.1 (7 minutes on site, two calls), but R5 attributes the delay to the restaurant because actual preparation (31 minutes) exceeded the quoted 15-minute window, and R5 says R1.1 is then not applied. Refund due.
provenance.why_hard: Both the old 20-minute threshold and the courier-wait exception point to no refund; only the amended threshold plus the attribution clause together produce yes.

Porting desk note: outbound port request for number ending 4471, account 33-90817

The customer requested yesterday that the number be ported to another operator. The porting system has flagged the account with two markers: an outstanding balance of 43.00 from the last invoice, and an automatic "high usage" marker generated by the billing engine after the customer's data use in the last week exceeded three times their monthly average. The desk agent is unsure whether the port should proceed.

The Number Porting Procedure (NPP-4) provides at paragraph 2.1 that an outbound port is completed within one working day of a valid request. Paragraph 2.2 originally provided that where the account carries an outstanding balance, the port is completed only after the balance is cleared, and the customer is told to pay first. Paragraph 2.3 provides the exception: a port is refused where the account is subject to a fraud hold, and the customer is directed to the fraud team; the refusal is lifted only when the fraud team removes the hold.

Paragraph 2.6 deals with delayed ports: where a port has been outstanding for more than 5 working days for reasons attributable to us, the customer is entitled to escalate to the regulator's porting dispute scheme and we must provide the reference number on request. This paragraph is about delay remedies and does not decide whether a port should proceed.

Paragraph 2.9 (definitions) states that "fraud hold" means a hold placed on the account by the fraud team and recorded with a fraud case number. Automatic markers generated by the billing engine, including "high usage", "credit review" and "roaming alert", are not fraud holds and do not by themselves prevent any account action.

Procedure Update NPP-4/U2, effective 1 March 2026, deleted the requirement in paragraph 2.2 that the balance be cleared before porting. Under the amended 2.2, the port proceeds and any outstanding balance, together with early termination charges if applicable, is billed to the customer on the final invoice.

The account record shows no fraud case number and no note from the fraud team. The request was made on 8 April 2026.

question.instructions: Determine how the porting desk should handle this request under NPP-4 as updated.

criteria.port_within_one_working_day: Complete the port within one working day and bill any balance on the final invoice.
criteria.port_after_balance_cleared: Complete the port only after the customer pays the outstanding balance.
criteria.refuse_port_fraud_hold: Refuse the port and direct the customer to the fraud team.
criteria.refuse_port_minimum_term: Refuse the port because the customer is within a minimum term.
criteria.escalate_to_regulator_scheme: Escalate the request to the regulator's porting dispute scheme.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The high-usage marker is a billing-engine marker, which 2.9 says is not a fraud hold; there is no fraud case number, so 2.3 does not apply. The balance no longer blocks the port after U2 (request made April 2026); it is billed on the final invoice. Nothing in the procedure refuses a port for a minimum term. 2.6 concerns escalation after delay, which has not occurred. The port proceeds within one working day.
provenance.why_hard: Two flags on the account both look like grounds to stop the port; one is neutralised by the definition and the other by the update.

Fleet operations note: fuel reimbursement claim from driver K. Brannigan, van reg. FL-2231

The driver submitted a personal-card fuel receipt for 96.40 on 12 July 2026, stating that the fleet fuel card was declined at the pump on 3 July 2026 and that he paid himself to finish the route. He asks for reimbursement through payroll.

The Fleet Fuel Card Procedure (FFP-3) governs. Paragraph 2 provides that a driver who pays for fuel personally because the fleet card was declined at the point of sale is reimbursed in full on production of the receipt, provided the receipt is submitted within 7 days of the purchase. Paragraph 2 was amended by Fleet Bulletin 26-07, effective 1 July 2026, which extended the submission period to 14 days to account for drivers on multi-day routes; the bulletin changes nothing else in paragraph 2.

Paragraph 3 sets out the exception: no reimbursement is made where the decline resulted from the card being suspended, because a suspension is notified to the driver in advance and the driver is expected to arrange fuel through the depot. Paragraph 3 refers to paragraph 9 for what counts as a suspension.

Paragraph 6 deals with personal mileage: fuel used for authorised private use of a fleet vehicle is deducted from salary at the published rate per mile, and receipts for private-use fuel are never reimbursable. This paragraph is about private mileage, not about declined cards.

Paragraph 9 (definitions) states that a card is "suspended" when it has been blocked by the fleet office, or when it has been blocked automatically by the card system following two consecutive missed weekly odometer submissions. An automatic block is treated as a suspension notified to the driver, because the card system sends a warning text after the first missed submission.

The fleet office checked the card system log for FL-2231. The weekly odometer submissions for the weeks beginning 15 June and 22 June 2026 are both missing. The system sent a warning text on 22 June and applied an automatic block on 29 June. The card was reactivated on 6 July after the driver submitted both readings. The route on 3 July was entirely business mileage; there is no private use recorded. The receipt was submitted 9 days after purchase.

question.instructions: Decide whether the driver's fuel receipt is reimbursable under FFP-3. Answer yes if reimbursable, no if not.

criteria.true: The personal fuel purchase must be reimbursed under the procedure.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The receipt was submitted 9 days after purchase, which is in time under the amended 14-day period. But paragraph 3 denies reimbursement where the decline resulted from a suspension, and paragraph 9 treats an automatic block after two consecutive missed odometer submissions as a suspension; the log shows exactly that (weeks of 15 and 22 June missed, block on 29 June, decline on 3 July). Paragraph 6 on private mileage is irrelevant since the route was business use. Not reimbursable.
provenance.why_hard: The amended deadline is satisfied and the trip was genuine business mileage, so the claim looks routine until the definition of suspension is applied to the card log.

Customer relations memo: seat move complaint, Meridian Theatre, performance of 2 June 2026

A customer bought two seats in row F for the 2 June performance. Four days before the performance the theatre emailed to say that a change to the set required the removal of rows E to G, and that the customer had been moved to two seats in row M. The customer has asked for compensation, stating that row M is "clearly worse" and that she received very little notice.

The Ticketing Conditions (TC-5) govern. Condition 9.1 provides that where the theatre reallocates a customer's seats to a lower category than the category purchased, the difference in price between the categories is refunded. Condition 9.2 provides an exception for production changes: where the reallocation is due to a production change and the customer is notified at least 7 days before the performance, the customer may instead choose a full refund of the tickets and not attend. Condition 9.4 provides that where a seat is sold as "restricted view" at a reduced price, no reallocation compensation is payable in respect of the restriction itself; the customer's seats were not sold as restricted view and 9.4 has no application.

Condition 9.8 (definitions) provides that "category" means the price band shown on the seat map at the time of purchase, and that seats in the same price band are of the same category whatever their row letter or distance from the stage.

Conditions Update TC-5/U1, effective 1 January 2026, added condition 9.3: where a reallocation to a lower category is notified fewer than 7 days before the performance, the customer receives the price difference plus 20% of the price paid, and 9.2's full-refund option is also available.

The seat map at the time of purchase shows rows D to N inclusive as price band B at 48 per seat, with rows A to C as band A at 65 and rows O to T as band C at 32. Rows F and M are both within band B. The customer paid 96 for the two seats. The box office assistant's draft reply offers the 20% uplift under 9.3 "since we gave under a week's notice".

question.instructions: Determine the compensation the conditions require for this reallocation.

criteria.price_difference_refund: The price difference between categories is refunded.
criteria.price_difference_plus_20_percent: The price difference plus 20% of the price paid is refunded.
criteria.full_refund_customer_choice: The customer may choose a full refund and not attend.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: Under 9.8 category is the price band at purchase, and rows F and M are both band B at 48. There is therefore no reallocation to a lower category, so 9.1 is not triggered, and 9.3 (which builds on a reallocation to a lower category) does not apply either; the short notice is irrelevant without a category drop. 9.2 also requires a lower-category reallocation and 7 days' notice, neither present. 9.4 is not engaged. No compensation is payable.
provenance.why_hard: The short notice fits the new 9.3 uplift and the assistant has already offered it; the definition of category removes the premise.

state:
Partner support note: review appeal from Sakura Bowl, review ID RV-2288104

Sakura Bowl has appealed a one-star review that reads in full: "Forty-five minutes late, food arrived cold, and the courier was rude when I asked why." The restaurant says none of this is about its cooking and asks for the review to be taken off its page.

The Review Standards (RS-3) govern. Under paragraph 4.1, a customer review remains on the partner's page unless it breaches the content rules in paragraph 6 (abuse, discrimination, personal data, or spam). Paragraph 4.2 originally provided the delivery exception: where a review concerns only delivery matters, the partner may request that the review be removed from its page, since delivery is performed by the platform's couriers and not by the partner. Paragraph 6.4 provides that reviews containing abusive language directed at a named individual are escalated to the trust team, which may remove the review and contact the reviewer; the review under appeal names no one and contains no abusive language, so paragraph 6.4 is not engaged.

Paragraph 4.7 (definitions) provides that a review "concerns only delivery matters" where every complaint in it relates to courier conduct, lateness, or the condition of the food on arrival that results from transit, and none relates to the preparation, taste, portion or accuracy of the food. The paragraph states expressly that the temperature of food on arrival is treated as a transit matter, not a preparation matter, unless the review says the food was cold when collected.

Standards Update RS-3/U2, effective 1 February 2026, replaced paragraph 4.2. Under the new paragraph 4.2, a review that concerns only delivery matters is not removed from the partner's page; instead its star rating is excluded from the partner's displayed score and the review is shown with a "delivery feedback" tag. The removal remedy no longer exists for delivery-only reviews.

The support agent's first response to the restaurant read: "Cold food is a food quality issue so the review stays and counts." The restaurant has escalated.

question.instructions: Determine the correct handling of this review under RS-3 as updated.

criteria.remove_review_from_page: Remove the review from the partner's page.
criteria.keep_review_and_count_rating: Keep the review and include its rating in the partner's score.
criteria.keep_review_exclude_rating: Keep the review with a delivery tag and exclude its rating from the score.
criteria.remove_review_and_warn_reviewer: Remove the review and issue a warning to the reviewer.
criteria.escalate_to_trust_team: Escalate the review to the trust team for content review.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: The review complains of lateness, cold food on arrival, and courier rudeness. Under 4.7 all three are delivery matters, cold-on-arrival being expressly a transit matter since the review does not say the food was cold at collection. It therefore concerns only delivery matters. After U2 the remedy is no longer removal but keeping the review with a delivery tag and excluding its rating from the score. No abusive language or named individual, so 6.4 does not apply.
provenance.why_hard: The restaurant's request matches the original removal remedy and the agent's reply reflects the intuition that cold food is a kitchen matter; both are displaced by the update and the definition.

Partner operations memo: disputed handover penalty, Bao Corner, order QK-4471

Bao Corner has disputed a 5 handover penalty applied to order QK-4471 on 24 June 2026, saying the courier arrived before the order was due and the restaurant should not be penalised for a courier who turns up early.

The Partner Service Standard (PSS-4) is the governing document. Under paragraph 3.1, a partner is charged a handover penalty of 5 for each order where the courier waits more than 10 minutes at the restaurant between arrival and handover. Paragraph 3.2 provides the exception: no penalty is charged where the courier arrived before the "ready by" time shown to the partner on the order screen, because a partner cannot be expected to hand over an order before it is due. Paragraph 3.5 is a separate provision about partner-initiated cancellations: a partner who cancels an accepted order is charged 3 and the customer is refunded in full; it does not apply to QK-4471, which was fulfilled.

Paragraph 3.8 defines courier arrival. The arrival time is the time the courier taps "arrived" in the courier app while inside the 50-metre geofence around the restaurant. A tap made outside the geofence is disregarded, and in that case arrival is set to the time of the courier's first location ping inside the geofence. The paragraph notes that the rule exists because some couriers tap "arrived" while still parking or queuing at another restaurant.

Standard Amendment SA-2026-06, effective 1 June 2026, changed paragraph 3.1 by replacing "more than 10 minutes" with "more than 8 minutes". Paragraph 3.2 and 3.8 were not changed.

The order data are as follows. Ready-by time shown to Bao Corner: 18:30. The courier tapped "arrived" at 18:27 from a position 300 metres from the restaurant, which the app recorded as outside the geofence. The courier's first location ping inside the geofence was at 18:33. The partner marked the order handed over at 18:43, and the courier's pickup confirmation is also 18:43. The restaurant's own note says the bao were "boxed and on the counter by 18:35".

question.instructions: Decide whether the 5 handover penalty is correctly charged to Bao Corner under PSS-4 as amended. Answer yes if the penalty stands, no if it should be removed.

criteria.false: The penalty should not have been charged.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-eval-mixed
provenance.rationale: Under 3.8 the 18:27 tap is disregarded because it was outside the geofence; arrival is the first in-geofence ping at 18:33. Handover was at 18:43, so the courier waited 10 minutes, which exceeds the amended 8-minute threshold in 3.1 (SA-2026-06 applies to a 24 June order). The 3.2 exception needs arrival before the 18:30 ready-by time, but 18:33 is after it. 3.5 does not apply. The penalty stands.
provenance.why_hard: The raw 'arrived' tap at 18:27 precedes the ready-by time and would trigger the exception; the geofence definition replaces that timestamp.
